summary: A 1977 specification for the Network Voice Protocol, an early scheme for sending digitised speech over a packet network. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a voice call over a computer network, cut into tiny pieces that are put back together at the other end.

questions: what is the network voice protocol
how did nvp handle packet loss
when was voice first sent over a packet network
subtitle: The first protocol for sending real-time voice conversations over a packet network

tldr.problem: The ARPANET was designed for data transfer, but there was a need for real-time interactive voice communication that would work reliably across the network.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Voice Protocol separates connection setup and negotiation (control protocol) from voice data transmission (data protocol), using different links for each and supporting multiple voice encoding schemes like LPC.
tldr.outcome: NVP enabled the first demonstration of secure, high-quality, full-duplex voice communication over a packet-switched network, implemented at multiple sites including ISI, Lincoln Laboratory, and Stanford Research Institute starting in 1973.

today: RFC 741 documents the first protocol for real-time voice over packet networks. Its principles—separating control from data, handling loss without retransmission, and adapting parameters on the fly—remain fundamental to modern voice protocols like RTP.

sections.title: Network Voice over ARPANET
sections.content:
The ARPANET's host protocol was optimized for data transfer, but as time went on, there was growing demand for real-time interactive voice communication across the network. RFC 741 specifies the Network Voice Protocol (NVP), designed by Danny Cohen at ISI starting in 1973. NVP addresses the fundamental mismatch between the data-focused HOST protocol and the needs of voice communication: it must handle message loss gracefully, avoid retransmission delays, and adapt to changing network conditions.

The protocol's design separates concerns cleanly: a control protocol handles connection setup and negotiation, while a separate data protocol carries the digitized voice.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice communication is different from sending files. You can't just retransmit voice if packets get lost—you need to skip ahead. NVP was the first protocol that got this right.

sections.title: Control and Data Separation
sections.content:
NVP uses four parallel links for each voice call: two for control messages (one from caller to answerer, one in reply) and two for voice data (one in each direction). Connection begins on a well-known link (377 octal) where the caller identifies both parties and proposes a link number. The answerer either refuses or accepts and assigns a reply link. Once links are agreed, both parties enter negotiation, where one party (typically the answerer) proposes voice encoding parameters and the other party accepts or rejects them.

The negotiation covers encoding scheme (LPC or CVSD), sample rate, version, maximum message length, and other codec-specific parameters. After negotiation succeeds, the call transitions to READY state and voice data begins flowing.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up the call is separate from sending voice. First you agree on a phone line (the links), then you agree on how to encode the voice (LPC or CVSD), then you talk.

sections.title: Voice Data and Encoding
sections.content:
Voice is encoded and sent in parcels, each representing a frame of speech at an agreed sample interval. For LPC (Linear Predictive Coding, the primary scheme), Version 1 uses 150-microsecond samples with 128 samples per frame, yielding a 19.2-millisecond frame time. Each data message carries a 32-bit header with a time stamp (sequence number), a bit indicating whether frames were skipped during silence, and a count of parcels in the message.

LPC encodes speech parameters as pointers into shared tables, allowing different accuracy levels through table selection. The protocol supports both simple encoding (sending all parameters every frame) and optimized encoding (sending only necessary updates). At any point, either party can request renegotiation to change encoding parameters, allowing adaptation to network conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice is broken into tiny sound chunks (parcels) of about 20 milliseconds each. Each chunk is coded using tables that both computers agreed on, so it can be very compact. If the network gets bad, you can negotiate better settings on the fly.

sections.title: Deployment and Reliability
sections.content: By the time RFC 741 was published in 1977, NVP had already been running for several years at multiple ARPANET sites: Information Sciences Institute (using LPC and CVSD), Lincoln Laboratory, Stanford Research Institute, and Culler-Harrison Inc. The protocol was designed to recover gracefully from message loss (silent skips rather than requests for retransmission), prevent one host from tying up another's resources, and minimize delay. The separation of control and data flows, combined with the header's time-stamp mechanism, allows receivers to detect lost packets and skip ahead rather than waiting for retransmission.
sections.plainLanguage: When some voice packets got lost, the system just skipped ahead instead of asking to resend them—important because asking for a retransmit would make the delay too long for a real conversation.
